receipt.public_excerpt: supportive comments boosted perceived consensus and made participants more likely to say they supported the basic argument made in the blog post, while critical comments had the opposite effects — regardless of the content of the post.

evidence_items.explanation: In this experiment, fabricated unanimous comment streams, including contrarian ones against the scientific consensus, shifted readers' sense of what most people think. That is the social-evidence mechanism the claim describes.

evidence_items.publisher: European Journal of Information Systems (via University of Edinburgh Research Explorer)

receipt.public_excerpt: bot participation by as little as 2–4% of a communication network can be sufficient to tip over the opinion climate in two out of three cases. These findings demonstrate a mechanism by which bots could shape the norms adopted by social media users.

evidence_items.explanation: A peer-reviewed model based on observed individual behavior shows that a small share of bots can flip the perceived opinion climate. This supports the claim that bots can make a minority view look dominant.

unresolved_gaps: No field study was found that directly measures AI bot swarms making a fringe view look like the majority view on real platforms.
The comment-stream experiment used human-written fabricated comments, not bots. The bot evidence comes from a simulation.
